prompt: What is the difference between `dpkg` and `apt`?
hint: One of them knows where packages come from.

choices.text: `apt` is the newer command and `dpkg` is deprecated
choices.why: Both are current, and `apt` calls `dpkg` to do the actual work.

choices.text: `apt` handles `.deb` files and `dpkg` handles repositories
choices.why: It is the other way round, which is worth getting straight before the rest of the lesson.

choices.text: `dpkg` handles one package file; `apt` knows the repositories
choices.why: Right — two layers, and `apt` runs `dpkg` underneath.

choices.text: `dpkg` is for system packages alone
choices.why: Both work on any package; the split is about fetching and resolving, not about who asked.

prompt: A one-line `apt install` downloaded forty megabytes for a small utility. Which field explains it?
hint: One of the relationship fields is installed by default and is not required.

choices.text: `Depends`, necessarily
choices.why: It can, and `Depends` is the required set, which is not what the flag below turns off.

choices.text: `Suggests`, when asked for
choices.why: `Suggests` is mentioned and never installed automatically.

choices.text: `Pre-Depends`, first
choices.why: Pre-Depends changes the ordering, not the size of the set.

choices.text: `Recommends`, on by default
choices.why: Right — and `--no-install-recommends` is the flag that turns it off.

prompt: A package goes from `3.03+dfsg2-7` to `3.03+dfsg2-8`. What changed?
hint: Three parts, and only one of them moved.

choices.text: The packaging, not the program
choices.why: Right — a patch, a build fix or a backported security change, with upstream untouched.

choices.text: The program, from 7 to 8
choices.why: The upstream version is the `3.03` at the front, and it is the same.

choices.text: Little; it is a build counter
choices.why: It counts packaging attempts, and a new one is frequently a backported security fix.

choices.text: The distribution removed something
choices.why: That is what the `+dfsg2` marker records, and it did not change either.

prompt: List what is inside a `.deb` without installing it: `dpkg ____ thing.deb`
hint: One letter, lowercase, and it is the same letter `tar` uses for the same job.

prompt: You run `apt upgrade` and it reports nothing to do, but you know a new version was released this morning. What did you forget?
hint: One command downloads a catalogue and the other acts on it.

choices.text: `apt full-upgrade`, to allow removals
choices.why: That matters when packages are held back, and here nothing was even offered.

choices.text: `apt update`, for current indexes
choices.why: Right — `upgrade` acted on yesterday's catalogue, correctly.

choices.text: `apt-mark unhold`, in case of a hold
choices.why: A hold is possible, and the first thing to rule out costs one command and no guessing.

choices.text: `apt clean`, to drop the cached one
choices.why: The cache holds downloaded files and is not consulted to decide what is available.

prompt: `apt update` prints `E: The repository ... is no longer signed.` What do you check first?
hint: That message names a consequence. The cause is one line above it.

choices.text: Whether the signing key expired, with `apt-key list`
choices.why: That is one cause of several, and `apt-key` is the deprecated tool it is not checked with.

choices.text: Whether the repository still exists
choices.why: Worth doing eventually, and apt already printed the server's answer.

choices.text: The `E: Failed to fetch` line above it, for the HTTP code
choices.why: Right — a `403` or `404` is a network answer, and a key problem says `NO_PUBKEY` instead.

choices.text: Whether `signed-by=` is present in the source file
choices.why: Its absence is a configuration style question rather than a cause of this error.

prompt: What does `signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc` in a source line accomplish?
hint: Think about what a key in the old global keyring could do.

choices.text: It encrypts the connection
choices.why: HTTPS does that, and it is a different property from a signature.

choices.text: It signs packages from there
choices.why: The repository's publisher signs them; your machine only verifies.

choices.text: It records the key used
choices.why: It is consulted at every update rather than written down after the fact.

choices.text: It limits that key to that one repository
choices.why: Right — a key in the old global keyring could vouch for any repository configured.

prompt: Match each word in an `apt update` listing to what it means.
hint: Three outcomes for one repository each.

pairs.right: it did not work, and E: says why

prompt: Print what `apt upgrade` would do, without doing it: `apt list ____`
hint: One long flag, and it is a single word after the dashes.

prompt: `0 upgraded, 2 newly installed, 4 to remove and 168 not upgraded.` Which number should stop you?
hint: Three of the four are routine. One is the machine telling you something is being taken away.

choices.text: `4 to remove`
choices.why: Right — satisfying the request needs four packages gone, and that is worth reading before `y`.

choices.text: `168 not upgraded`
choices.why: It is, and that is a separate job; it has nothing to do with this install.

choices.text: `2 newly installed`
choices.why: That is normal: the extra one is a dependency, listed above.

choices.text: `0 upgraded`, which is wrong
choices.why: An install only upgrades a dependency when the requested version needs it to.

prompt: Why does `apt` print `WARNING: apt does not have a stable CLI interface` when its output goes into a pipe?
hint: Two commands do this job and only one of them promises not to change.

choices.text: Because piping apt's output is unsupported entirely
choices.why: It works; the warning is about relying on the exact text in the long term.

choices.text: Because `apt` reserves the right to change its output
choices.why: Right — `apt` is for people, `apt-get` and `apt-cache` for scripts.

choices.text: Because apt drops its progress bars in a pipe, and wants to say so
choices.why: It quietly drops them; the warning is about the interface rather than the display.

choices.text: Because it may need a terminal for the confirmation prompt
choices.why: `-y` handles that, and the warning appears for commands that never prompt.

prompt: What is the difference between the `Unpacking` and `Setting up` lines of an install?
hint: One writes files and the other runs something.

choices.text: `Unpacking` extracts the archive and `Setting up` verifies the checksums
choices.why: Verification happens before either, when the download is checked against the index.

choices.text: `Unpacking` is the dependency and `Setting up` is the package you asked for
choices.why: Both lines appear for every package, dependencies included.

choices.text: `Unpacking` writes the files; `Setting up` runs the package's own setup
choices.why: Right, and a package can be stuck between the two — section 109's `iU`.

choices.text: `Unpacking` is done by apt and `Setting up` by systemd
choices.why: dpkg does both; systemd is involved only if the package starts a service.

prompt: Install without pulling in the optional extras: `apt install ____ thing`
hint: One long flag, three words joined by dashes.

prompt: A config file appeared in `/etc` and you do not know what wrote it. One command.
hint: The package manager wrote down what it installed.

choices.text: `apt search`, by name
choices.why: `apt search` matches names and descriptions of packages, not the files inside them.

choices.text: `apt-file search` on the path
choices.why: That asks the repositories about packages you have not installed, which is the other direction.

choices.text: `find / -newer`
choices.why: That finds files with similar timestamps and never names a package.

choices.text: `dpkg -S /etc/thatfile`
choices.why: Right — a database lookup, and it answers instantly.

prompt: `dpkg -S /usr/local/bin/mytool` prints `no path found matching pattern`. What does that tell you?
hint: Lesson 3 named that directory for a reason.

choices.text: The dpkg database is out of date
choices.why: The database is fine; it simply has no row for that path, which is an answer.

choices.text: No package installed it, so nothing will upgrade or remove it
choices.why: Right — `/usr/local` is for software installed outside the package manager.

choices.text: The file is a symlink, and `dpkg -S` cannot follow one
choices.why: `dpkg -S` matches the path as recorded; a symlink installed by a package is found.

choices.text: You need `sudo` to read the package database
choices.why: It is world-readable, and a permission problem reports differently.

prompt: `bash: pdftotext: command not found`, and you do not know which package has it. What do you use?
hint: The file is not on the machine, so the machine's own database cannot help.

choices.text: `apt-file search bin/pdftotext`
choices.why: Right — it searches the repositories' file lists, which is what `dpkg -S` cannot do.

choices.text: `dpkg -S $(which pdftotext)`
choices.why: `which` finds nothing, so there is no path to look up.

choices.text: `apt search pdftotext`
choices.why: Sometimes it does, and a file that is not in any description is not found at all.

choices.text: `dpkg -L poppler-utils`, if you guessed
choices.why: That works after the guess, and the guess is the part you needed help with.

prompt: Match each question to the command that answers it.
hint: Four questions that sound alike and are not.

pairs.left: which package would give me this file

prompt: Search for a package by exactly that name and nothing else: `apt search "____ripgrep$"`
hint: One character, and it is the regular-expression anchor for the start of a string.

prompt: You are about to `apt remove` a library on a production machine. What do you run first?
hint: Two commands answer it; one asks the repositories and one asks this machine.

choices.text: `apt-cache depends libfoo`
choices.why: That lists what the library itself needs, which is the wrong direction.

choices.text: `dpkg -L libfoo` to see what it owns
choices.why: The file list does not say which other packages would break.

choices.text: `apt-get remove --dry-run libfoo`
choices.why: Right — it prints the exact plan, including anything that comes with it, and changes nothing.

choices.text: `apt-mark showauto`
choices.why: That says how it got there rather than what depends on it now.

prompt: `apt-cache rdepends libfoo` lists three packages, but `--dry-run` on removing it takes away only one. Why?
hint: The two commands are asking different populations.

choices.text: `rdepends` includes Recommends, and `--dry-run` counts Depends alone
choices.why: `rdepends` does report the relationship type when asked, and the count here is about something else.

choices.text: `rdepends` covers the repositories; one of the three is here
choices.why: Right — read `rdepends` as who could care, and `--dry-run` as what would happen here.

choices.text: `rdepends` includes the package itself, so the real count is two
choices.why: It does print the name at the top, and that accounts for one line and not two.

choices.text: `--dry-run` stops at the first package it would remove
choices.why: It prints the complete plan; that is what makes it useful.

prompt: You installed A, which pulled in B. You removed A but you use B directly. How do you stop `autoremove` taking B?
hint: apt records why each package is there, and the record can be corrected.

choices.text: `apt-mark hold B`
choices.why: A hold stops upgrades and does not stop autoremove from removing it.

choices.text: Reinstall B with `apt install B`, which resets the mark
choices.why: Installing a package that is already installed leaves the mark as it is.

choices.text: Add B to `/etc/apt/preferences.d/`
choices.why: Pins change which version is chosen, not whether a package is wanted.

choices.text: `apt-mark manual B`
choices.why: Right — that says somebody wants it, regardless of what needs it.

prompt: `somepackage : Depends: libsomething (>= 2.0) but 1.9 is to be installed`. What usually causes this?
hint: Read the two version numbers, and ask where each one came from.

choices.text: A package built for another release
choices.why: Right — a `.deb` for a newer version, or a third-party repository assuming another base.

choices.text: An interrupted install, which `--fix-broken` repairs
choices.why: That produces unconfigured packages rather than an unsatisfiable version constraint.

choices.text: A held package
choices.why: A hold keeps a package where it is and does not create this message.

choices.text: A stale index needing `apt update`
choices.why: Worth ruling out first, and a fresh index rarely turns 1.9 into 2.0.

prompt: Match each relationship field to what it means.
hint: Five of the seven; two of them are about things that cannot coexist or can substitute.

pairs.right: must be there, or this is not configured
mentioned, never installed on its own
a virtual name several packages can satisfy

right_distractors: installed before this one is unpacked
the same version must be used

prompt: `dpkg -l thing` shows `iU`. What has happened?
hint: Two letters, two steps of an install.

choices.text: It is installed and an upgrade is available
choices.why: `dpkg -l` reports state, not what the repositories offer; that is `apt policy`.

choices.text: It is installed and marked for upgrade at the next run
choices.why: Nothing queues an upgrade in the status column.

choices.text: Wanted installed; unpacked and not configured
choices.why: Right — the files exist and the package's setup never ran.

choices.text: It is installed and its user configuration has been changed
choices.why: A changed config file does not appear in the status letters at all.

prompt: Somebody sends you a `.deb`. Which command installs it with its dependencies?
hint: One of these two forms tells apt to treat a path as a package file.

choices.text: `dpkg -i ./thing.deb`
choices.why: dpkg installs it and does not fetch anything, which is the whole point of this section.

choices.text: `apt install ./thing.deb`
choices.why: Right — the `./` makes apt read it as a file, and it resolves dependencies as usual.

choices.text: `apt install thing.deb`
choices.why: Without a slash, apt looks for a package named `thing.deb` in the repositories.

choices.text: `apt-get download ./thing.deb`
choices.why: `download` fetches a package from a repository into the current directory.

prompt: An install was interrupted by a reboot. Packages are unpacked and unconfigured, and nothing is missing. Which repair?
hint: Two commands repair two different causes.

choices.text: `apt-get --fix-broken install` first
choices.why: That fetches what is missing, and by the premise nothing is.

choices.text: `apt-get purge` and install again
choices.why: That works and throws away configuration you did not have to lose.

choices.text: `dpkg -i` the packages again
choices.why: Reinstalling repeats the unpack, and the unpack is not the step that failed.

choices.text: `dpkg --configure -a`, to finish
choices.why: Right — it retries the configuration step for everything that is half done.

prompt: Fetch a package file into the current directory without installing it: `apt-get ____ cowsay`
hint: One word, eight letters.

prompt: `dpkg -l thing` shows `rc`. What is on the machine?
hint: Two letters: what is wanted, and what is true.

choices.text: Nothing; the row is left over and can be ignored
choices.why: The row exists because something does: the configuration files.

choices.text: Its configuration files, and nothing else
choices.why: Right — `remove` was used, so `/etc` still has its settings.

choices.text: The program, minus its config
choices.why: That is not a state dpkg can be in; the files go together with the package.

choices.text: A partial install that needs `dpkg --configure -a`
choices.why: That state is `iU`, with an uppercase second letter meaning something went wrong.

prompt: You removed a misconfigured service and reinstalled it. It came back with the same broken settings. Why?
hint: One of the two uninstall commands keeps something for you.

choices.text: The package cached its own configuration away in `/var/cache/apt`
choices.why: That directory holds downloaded `.deb` files, not settings.

choices.text: `autoremove` restored the old files when it ran
choices.why: `autoremove` removes packages; it puts nothing back.

choices.text: The reinstall pulled your settings from the repository
choices.why: Repositories carry a package's default files, not yours.

choices.text: `remove` kept the configuration, and the reinstall reused it
choices.why: Right — `purge` is the one that would have taken it away.

prompt: What does `apt autoremove` use to decide what to take?
hint: apt records something about every package at install time.

choices.text: The `auto` mark, and whether anything needs it
choices.why: Right — installed as a dependency, and nothing depends on it any more.

choices.text: The last access time recorded on the package's own files
choices.why: Nothing in apt looks at access times; many filesystems do not record them usefully.

choices.text: Whether it is in any index
choices.why: A package missing from the indexes is a different situation and is not removed for it.

choices.text: The `rc` state left behind by previous removals
choices.why: `rc` packages have no files to speak of, and `autoremove --purge` is what clears them.

prompt: List every package that has left configuration behind: `dpkg -l | grep '____rc'`
hint: One character: the regular-expression anchor for the start of a line.

prompt: A package will not upgrade, `apt upgrade` says nothing about it, and the version is months old. First command?
hint: Something can make apt skip a package silently.

choices.text: `apt policy`, to see the candidate
choices.why: Worth running second; it shows what is offered without saying why it is being skipped.

choices.text: `apt update`, for a stale index
choices.why: Cheap and worth doing, and a stale index would affect every package rather than one.

choices.text: `apt-mark showhold`, to see holds
choices.why: Right — a hold makes `upgrade` skip it without a word, and this is the only way to see one.

choices.text: `apt-cache rdepends`, for blockers
choices.why: That lists what depends on it, and a blocked upgrade is reported as `not upgraded` rather than silence.

prompt: In `apt policy`, what does `Candidate` mean?
hint: It is the newest of a set, and the set is narrower than you might think.

choices.text: The newest version the project has released
choices.why: apt has no idea what upstream released; it knows only what your repositories offer.

choices.text: The version `apt install` would give you now
choices.why: Right — newest among the configured repositories, at their priorities.

choices.text: The version that was installed most recently
choices.why: That is `Installed`, printed on the line above it.

choices.text: The version recommended by the distribution's maintainers
choices.why: There is no such field; priority is the mechanism and it is a number.

prompt: An installed package sits at priority 100. What does that number stop from happening?
hint: Repositories are 500. Ask what 500 beats and what it does not.

choices.text: It stops a routine autoremove
choices.why: The auto mark decides that; priorities are about which version wins.

choices.text: It stops third-party repositories from upgrading it
choices.why: A third-party repository is 500, which is higher, so it can and does.

choices.text: It stops the package from being upgraded by anything
choices.why: 500 beats 100, so a newer version from any normal repository is installed happily.

choices.text: It stops an older version replacing it on its own
choices.why: Right — nothing below 1000 can push an installed version out in favour of an older one.

prompt: Stop a package from being upgraded, without editing any file: `apt-mark ____ postgresql`
hint: One word, four letters.

prompt: On a Rocky Linux machine, somebody's notes say `yum install nginx`. Should you change it to `dnf`?
hint: Look up what `yum` is on a current Red Hat family system.

choices.text: Yes — `yum` was removed
choices.why: It is still there and still works; it was kept precisely so notes like these keep working.

choices.text: Yes — `yum` resolves them differently
choices.why: There is one resolver, and both names reach it.

choices.text: No — `yum` is a symlink to `dnf`
choices.why: Right, and typing either is fine.

choices.text: No — RHEL against Fedora
choices.why: Both names work on both; the split is historical rather than by distribution.

prompt: Why is there no `dnf update` step before `dnf install`, the way `apt update` comes before `apt install`?
hint: One of the two refreshes itself.

choices.text: dnf downloads the list each time
choices.why: It uses a cache; re-downloading each time would make every command slow.

choices.text: dnf reads the repositories live
choices.why: It caches; the difference is when the cache is considered stale.

choices.text: dnf has no index
choices.why: It has metadata, and `dnf makecache` is the command that builds it.

choices.text: dnf expires its own metadata
choices.why: Right — `Last metadata expiration check` is the line that reports it.

prompt: You press Return at `Is this ok [y/N]:` in dnf, out of habit from apt. What happens?
hint: Read which letter is capitalised.

choices.text: Nothing is installed; the capital `N` is the default
choices.why: Right — apt's `[Y/n]` and zypper's `(y)` go the other way.

choices.text: It installs, since Return accepts in every package manager
choices.why: It does in two of the three, which is exactly why this catches people.

choices.text: It asks again, since Return is not a valid answer
choices.why: Return is valid and means the capitalised option.

choices.text: It shows the full version list, which is what `v` does
choices.why: That is zypper's prompt, and it needs the letter typed.

prompt: Match each `rpm` query to its Debian equivalent.
hint: Five queries, and every one of them starts with `-q`.

prompt: `rpm -i pkg.rpm` fails with `Failed dependencies`. How does that differ from `dpkg -i` failing the same way?
hint: One of them has already written to the disk by the time it complains.

choices.text: rpm leaves the package unpacked; dpkg refuses outright
choices.why: It is the other way round, and the difference matters when you go looking for the damage.

choices.text: rpm writes nothing; dpkg unpacks and leaves it unconfigured
choices.why: Right — there is no rpm equivalent of `iU` to clean up afterwards.

choices.text: Both write nothing, and the two messages are just worded differently
choices.why: dpkg's message says `leaving unconfigured`, which is it telling you it wrote files.

choices.text: rpm retries against the repositories; dpkg has none to try
choices.why: `rpm -i` is the low layer and does not know about repositories either.

prompt: After a large `dnf upgrade`, what should you look for in `/etc`?
hint: rpm does not ask about configuration the way Debian does; it leaves something instead.

choices.text: Packages in the `rc` state
choices.why: `rc` is a dpkg status and has no rpm equivalent.

choices.text: Config files with no owner
choices.why: Worth doing once in a while, and it is not what an upgrade leaves behind.

choices.text: `.rpmnew` and `.rpmsave` files
choices.why: Right — the packagers' new version beside yours, or yours moved aside.

choices.text: Files newer than the upgrade itself
choices.why: That finds everything the upgrade touched, including the many files with no decision to make.

prompt: Ask dnf which package ships a given path, quoting so the shell leaves it alone: `dnf ____ '*/bin/pdftotext'`
hint: One word, eight letters.

prompt: You run openSUSE Tumbleweed and have used `zypper up` every month for a year. What is the problem?
hint: A rolling release replaces whole sets of packages at once.

choices.text: Little; `up` is the routine command on most systems
choices.why: It is on Leap and SLES, and Tumbleweed is the distribution that differs.

choices.text: `up` refuses vendor changes, so the machine is half-upgraded
choices.why: Right — `dup` is the routine command on a rolling release, and `up` is not.

choices.text: `up` upgrades everything including the kernel, which needs a reboot first
choices.why: A kernel upgrade wants a reboot afterwards on any distribution, and that is not this.

choices.text: `up` applies security patches alone, which is `zypper patch`
choices.why: `patch` is the patches-only command; `up` does ordinary version upgrades.

prompt: In `zypper search` output, what is the difference between `i` and `i+` in the `S` column?
hint: One of the two is a package somebody typed the name of.

choices.text: `i+` means an upgrade is available for it
choices.why: Availability is what `zypper list-updates` reports, in a different listing.

choices.text: `i+` means it is installed from a third-party repository
choices.why: The repository appears in `zypper info`, not as a plus in the status column.

choices.text: `i+` means it is locked against upgrades
choices.why: Locks show in `zypper locks`; the status column does not carry them.

choices.text: `i+` was asked for; plain `i` came in as a dependency
choices.why: Right — the same distinction as apt's manual and auto marks.

prompt: What does `zypper ps` report, and why does it matter after an upgrade?
hint: Section 98's open descriptors, used on purpose.

choices.text: Processes using files that were replaced
choices.why: Right — they are running code that no longer exists on disk, and need restarting.

choices.text: Processes the upgrade started
choices.why: Being newly installed does not make a process interesting; still holding old files does.

choices.text: Packages whose services failed to restart
choices.why: That is `systemctl --failed`, and it is a different question.

choices.text: Processes holding the database lock
choices.why: A held lock is reported when zypper cannot start, with a different message.

prompt: The two-letter short form of `zypper install`, which is what SUSE documentation uses: `zypper ____ nginx`
hint: Two letters, and they are the middle of the word it stands for.

prompt: You are on an unfamiliar distribution and about to run an upgrade command you half remember. What do you do first?
hint: All three managers have the same escape hatch.

choices.text: Run it and read the confirmation prompt
choices.why: Reasonable on two of the three, and dnf's prompt defaults to no while the others default to yes.

choices.text: Check `/etc/os-release` to identify the distribution
choices.why: Worth knowing and it does not tell you what the command would do.

choices.text: Ask it to print the plan without acting
choices.why: Right: `apt --dry-run`, `dnf --assumeno`, `zypper install --dry-run`.

choices.text: Look for the transaction log, so you can undo it afterwards
choices.why: Only dnf can undo, and undoing is worse than not doing.

prompt: Which of these has no equivalent on the rpm side?
hint: It is the one about what is left behind after an uninstall.

choices.text: `apt autoremove`
choices.why: `dnf autoremove` is the same idea with the same name.

choices.text: `apt purge`
choices.why: Right — rpm has no `rc` state; it leaves `.rpmsave` files instead.

choices.text: `apt policy`
choices.why: `dnf --showduplicates list` answers the same question about versions.

choices.text: `apt-file search`
choices.why: `dnf provides` does it, and without the extra index download.

prompt: Match each apt command to its dnf equivalent.
hint: Five pairs; one of the five needs no command at all on the dnf side.

prompt: `sudo pip install requests` on a system that allows it. What breaks, and when?
hint: Ask which directory it writes into, and who else writes there.

choices.text: A system tool in python, eventually
choices.why: Right — two package managers disagreeing about one directory, and the loser is usually not your project.

choices.text: Your own project, at once
choices.why: Your project gets the version you asked for; the damage lands elsewhere.

choices.text: Little, if the versions match
choices.why: The versions drift on the next upgrade, which is when it arrives.

choices.text: pip itself, for want of write access
choices.why: With `sudo` it writes fine, which is the whole problem.

prompt: `error: externally-managed-environment` from pip. What is the best response?
hint: The error text names three alternatives, in order.

choices.text: `pip install --break-system-packages`, which is what the flag is for
choices.why: The flag exists and is named after what it does; it is the last resort rather than the first.

choices.text: Remove the `EXTERNALLY-MANAGED` marker file
choices.why: That silences the check and leaves the collision it was warning about.

choices.text: Run it with `sudo`, which has the necessary permissions
choices.why: Permission was never the problem; the check is deliberate.

choices.text: The distribution's package, a venv, or pipx — in that order
choices.why: Right, and those are the three the error itself suggests.

prompt: Which of these are true of software installed into `/usr/local` by hand?
hint: Think about what the package database does and does not contain.

choices.text: `dpkg -S` on its files finds no package
choices.why: Yes — that empty answer is the definition of unmanaged.

choices.text: It is not upgraded when the machine is upgraded
choices.why: Yes, and it stays at the version you installed until you notice.

choices.text: `apt remove` cannot remove it
choices.why: Yes — apt has no record of it to act on.

choices.text: It is ignored by the shell's PATH by default
choices.why: `/usr/local/bin` is on the default PATH, which is why the binary works at all.

choices.text: It will conflict with a distribution package of the same name
choices.why: They coexist in different directories; which one runs is a PATH question.

prompt: Give a command-line tool its own environment and one entry on your PATH: `____ install ruff`
hint: Four letters, and it is pip's name with one more.

prompt: A colleague installed a `.deb` by hand and the program now fails with a library error. What do you check first?
hint: One command tells you whether the package finished installing.

choices.text: `ldd` on the binary, to see which library is missing
choices.why: That names the library and not the reason, and the reason is one letter away.

choices.text: `dpkg -l thatpackage`, for the two status letters
choices.why: Right — `iU` means unpacked and never configured, which is exactly this failure.

choices.text: The program's own log, for the version it thinks it has
choices.why: A half-configured package rarely logs anything useful, and often will not start to log.

choices.text: `apt update`, in case the index is stale
choices.why: The index has nothing to do with a package that is already on the disk.

prompt: Put these in the order you would work through installing something you have never installed before.
trap: Find out what version you would get, see the plan, do it, then find out where it went.

prompt: The disk is filling up on a machine that has been upgraded for years. Which of these frees space and loses nothing you need?
hint: Two of the four remove things that might matter.

choices.text: `apt purge` on the `rc` packages
choices.why: It does free space, and it also throws away configuration for software you may reinstall.

choices.text: `apt autoremove --purge`
choices.why: Useful and worth reading first; it removes packages, which is more than nothing.

choices.text: `apt clean`, the cache alone
choices.why: Right — it empties the cache of downloaded `.deb` files, which can be fetched again.

choices.text: `apt-mark showhold`, then unhold
choices.why: That changes nothing on disk and lets held packages upgrade, which uses more space.

prompt: You are writing a Dockerfile. Which line is wrong?
hint: One of these is the interactive habit, in a place where nobody is watching.

choices.text: `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl`
choices.why: That is the correct shape: update and install in one layer, recommends off, non-interactive.

choices.text: `RUN apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`
choices.why: That is the cleanup that keeps the image small.

choices.text: `RUN apt-get install -y ca-certificates`
choices.why: Acceptable after an update in the same layer, and the scripted command is the right one.

choices.text: `RUN apt install curl`
choices.why: Right — `apt` for scripts, and no `-y`, so the build stops at a prompt nobody can answer.

prompt: Match each symptom to the first command to run.
hint: Six symptoms from across the lesson.

pairs.left: a program fails looking for a library
command not found and no idea what to install
a config file you did not write
reinstalled and the old settings came back
is no longer signed after an update
pairs.right: read the E: Failed to fetch line

prompt: A third-party repository has started providing a newer version of a library your distribution also ships. What do you do about it?
hint: There is a file whose whole purpose is expressing this preference.

choices.text: Pin that origin below 500, so nothing comes from it unless asked
choices.why: Right — `Pin-Priority: 100` puts it under "already installed".

choices.text: Hold the library, so it stays where it is
choices.why: That fixes one package and leaves the next one the repository takes over.

choices.text: Disable the repository, and enable it only when installing from it
choices.why: It works and it means the thing you wanted from that repository stops upgrading too.

choices.text: Remove the library and install it from the third party deliberately
choices.why: That accepts the takeover rather than preventing it, for a package you did not choose them for.

prompt: `dnf remove openssl-libs` proposes to remove forty packages. What is it telling you?
hint: It resolved dependencies in the direction you did not ask about.

choices.text: Forty unused dependencies
choices.why: That is `autoremove`, and it is a separate command with a separate list.

choices.text: Forty installed packages require it and cannot stay
choices.why: Right — and this is the moment to press `n` and think.

choices.text: Forty packages provide the same capability and conflict
choices.why: Conflicts are reported as conflicts, and they are not removed in bulk.

choices.text: The transaction test failed and it is proposing a rollback
choices.why: The test runs after you confirm, and a rollback is `dnf history undo`.

prompt: Finish configuring every package that an interrupted install left half done: `dpkg --configure ____`
hint: A dash and one letter, meaning all of them.

prompt: Repair a package left unconfigured because a dependency was missing: `apt-get ____ install`
hint: Two words after the dashes, joined by one.

prompt: Put these in the order they happen when `apt install` runs on a package with one missing dependency.
items: apt resolves the dependency and prints the plan
dpkg configures the dependency, then the package
trap: Read, decide, fetch, write, run — and the dependency is configured before the thing that needs it.

prompt: The rpm-family command that answers "which package owns this file", on both dnf and zypper systems: `____ /usr/bin/ls`
hint: Two words: the low-layer tool and a query flag with one extra letter.

prompt: Which command changes nothing on the machine?
hint: Three of these four write something.

choices.text: `apt upgrade`
choices.why: It installs newer versions of everything installed, which is a great deal of change.

choices.text: `apt autoremove`
choices.why: It removes packages nothing needs any more.

choices.text: `apt update`
choices.why: Right — it refreshes the indexes in a cache and touches no installed package.

choices.text: `apt purge thing`
choices.why: It removes a package and its configuration files.

prompt: Somebody's runbook says `apt-key add` to trust a new repository. What do you do?
hint: That command was replaced, and the replacement is in the source line rather than a keyring.

choices.text: Run it; `apt-key` is the supported way to add a repository key
choices.why: It is deprecated, and a key added that way vouches for every repository on the machine.

choices.text: Run it with `sudo`, since keys are root-owned
choices.why: Permission is not the problem; the mechanism is.

choices.text: Skip the key entirely and add `[trusted=yes]` to the source line
choices.why: That disables verification, which is worse than the deprecated command.

choices.text: Put the key in `/etc/apt/keyrings/` and use `signed-by=`
choices.why: Right — one key, scoped to one repository, and the runbook is old enough to re-check.

prompt: You need the same software on a Debian machine and a Rocky machine. Which part of your notes transfers unchanged?
hint: One layer is shared between dnf and zypper, and one is not shared with Debian at all.

choices.text: The install command, low layer
choices.why: `dpkg -i` and `rpm -i` are different commands with different options and different behaviour on failure.

choices.text: The reasoning, not the words
choices.why: Right — verb, target, scope, dry-run, and a table to look the spelling up in.

choices.text: The queries themselves
choices.why: `rpm` can be installed on Debian and its database is empty of Debian packages.

choices.text: The repository file format
choices.why: `.repo` and `.list` are different formats with different field names.

prompt: Print what `apt install nginx` would do, without installing anything: `apt install ____ nginx`
hint: One long flag, two words joined by a dash.
